title: What Will the Policy Pay When the Facility Stops?
seoTitle: Texas Commercial Property Insurance: Coverage and Risk Diligence
subtitle: Compare the peril, valuation, deductible and interruption trigger before turning a Texas insurance quote into an operating assumption.
seoDescription: Review Texas commercial property insurance: wind and flood coverage, TWIA’s 2026 filings, business income, deductibles, surplus lines and facility risk.
author: Sulayman Bowles
evidenceBoundary: Primary insurance guidance, public filing records and sample commercial forms verified October 12, 2026. No actual facility, insurer quotation or claim outcome was verified. Hypothetical prices and losses are not commercial market estimates; residential data is not used to infer commercial premiums.
content: A commercial-property quote becomes useful when a business can explain what happens after a specific loss. Which property is damaged? What caused it? How is the damage valued? What portion stays with the business, and what pays while operations are suspended? The premium is only one input to that sequence.

A current Texas development shows why the distinction matters. TWIA’s board voted August 4, 2026 to file no rate change for 2027, and TDI lists the commercial filing as File and Use. That is evidence about one wind-and-hail insurer’s filing, not a promise that a facility’s total premium stays flat or that its recovery needs are covered. [Board action](#source-rate-action); [commercial filing record](#source-rate-register).

For a purchase, lease or renewal, compare policies against the same asset inventory and loss scenarios. The stronger insurance decision connects coverage to the business’s ability to recover, with enough liquidity for the exposures it retains.

sections.title: Start with the event and the actual insured property
paragraphs: TDI’s commercial guide distinguishes basic, broad and special forms, with special forms generally covering causes except listed exclusions. It identifies flood, earth movement and wear among common exclusions. A broad-sounding coverage label does not answer which events, property and conditions the issued contract covers. [Commercial-property guide](#source-commercial-guide).

Build an asset inventory by site: building, tenant improvements, production equipment, stock, property belonging to others, outdoor equipment and assets in transit. Reconcile it with the insured entity, locations and schedules. Ownership, possession and the obligation to repair can differ between landlord, tenant, equipment lessor and operating company.

Then test events relevant to the facility’s physical setting and operations: roof damage, rising water, freezing, fire, equipment failure, utility disruption and loss of access. These are suggested scenarios, not a measured ranking of Texas hazards. Use actual inspection, maintenance and site evidence to identify the pathways that could stop the business.

Keep the hazard and the insurance trigger distinct. A storm can cause both wind damage and flooding. The business needs to know which contract addresses each cause and whether a disputed or excluded cause leaves an important gap. A large overall limit cannot cure an excluded peril.

sections.title: Separate wind coverage from flood and the rest of the program
paragraphs: TWIA describes its coverage as wind and hail only for eligible properties in the designated catastrophe area. Its application requirements include a private-market declination, building-code certification with limited exceptions, underwriting criteria and proof of flood coverage when required. Being on the coast does not itself establish eligibility or an issued policy. [TWIA eligibility](#source-wind-eligibility).

The published commercial policy expressly excludes flood, surface water, storm surge and specified related water causes, whether driven by wind or not. It also has an off-premises utility-failure exclusion with a stated on-premises equipment exception. Those provisions illustrate why the actual cause and location of damage matter. The sample is evidence of that form, not a determination of coverage under a business’s issued policy. [Commercial form, exclusions](#source-commercial-form).

NFIP guidance publishes maximum non-residential limits of $500,000 for the building and $500,000 for contents. It excludes financial losses from business interruption or loss of use. The building and contents limits are separate; a business should not treat them as a freely interchangeable $1 million recovery pool. [NFIP coverage](#source-flood-coverage). The guidance also treats building and contents deductibles separately; preserve each in the recovery model.

Compare the limits and valuation terms with the property’s actual replacement and contents requirements. Ask about private or excess flood options where needed, without assuming their availability or price. Confirm binding and effective dates before the transaction or exposure begins. Flood requirements for a lender, TWIA eligibility and a prudent recovery plan can ask different questions.

sections.title: Normalize values and deductibles before comparing premiums
paragraphs: Replacement cost and actual cash value differ. TDI describes actual cash value as replacement cost less depreciation. An issued policy can combine settlement bases or attach conditions and endorsements. TWIA’s catalogue, for example, lists both commercial replacement-cost coverage and replacement cost excluding roof coverings. A title on the quote does not settle treatment of every asset. [Valuation guidance](#source-commercial-guide); [published endorsements](#source-form-catalogue).

Have the broker identify the valuation date, insured values, settlement conditions and any coinsurance or reporting provisions in the actual contract. A property’s purchase price, tax appraisal and accounting value answer different questions from the cost and conditions of insured repair. Keep those amounts separate in the site model; see the related [property-tax underwriting investigation](/research/texas/texas-property-tax-business-underwriting).

Percentage deductibles need a denominator and an application rule. Ask whether the percentage applies to one building, the affected location’s scheduled value, another stated amount or a different basis, and whether it applies per occurrence or separately by item. Calculate the result in dollars for the facility. A familiar percentage is not enough to assess liquidity.

The two hypothetical quotes below insure the same $12 million scheduled value. Assume Quote A explicitly applies a 3% deductible to that full value for the modeled wind event, and Quote B applies a $100,000 deductible. Assume a $600,000 physical loss is covered and agreed, with adequate limits and no depreciation, coinsurance or other restrictions. Prices and terms are invented comparison inputs, not available market offers.

sections.title: Price retained loss without inventing an expected-loss estimate
paragraphs: Quote A saves $30,000 annually while retaining $260,000 more in the modeled event. That additional retention equals about 8.7 years of the premium difference. It does not prove Quote B is better: no probability of loss, financing cost or alternate use of cash has been estimated. The comparison reveals the decision that a premium-only table hides.

Test smaller and larger losses as well. A loss below a deductible, an excluded cause and a loss above a sublimit produce different outcomes. Retained exposure can also accumulate across sites or events. Ask finance what liquidity is available at the same time a facility is losing income and paying recovery expenses.

Risk reduction belongs in the comparison. A roof improvement, drainage work, fire protection or protected placement of critical equipment could change physical damage or interruption consequences. Obtain evidence about the measure and ask how the insurer treats it. Do not book a discount or a reduction in event probability solely because an improvement appears in a plan.

The insurance and operating decisions should meet at one recovery schedule. Identify equipment lead times, repair access, qualification testing, inventory replacement and customer restart requirements. Coverage needs to be assessed against that sequence, not merely the date when walls and a roof are repaired.

sections.title: Read the suspension trigger and the time limit
paragraphs: TDI describes business-interruption coverage as generally following direct physical loss or damage from a covered peril, with policy wording controlling. Contingent interruption and civil-authority extensions have their own conditions. A supplier delay, government order or undamaged facility without power does not by itself establish a covered business-income claim. [Interruption guidance](#source-business-income).

TWIA’s currently linked TWIA-17 endorsement gives a concrete commercial example. It connects suspension to covered wind or hail damage at specified property, uses scheduled daily and total limits, and includes a 168-hour time deductible. Its extra-expense maximum is $10,000. The form is effective November 27, 2011 and remains in the current catalogue; it is not a new 2026 rule or proof that any policy includes the endorsement. [TWIA-17](#source-income-endorsement). The form waives another time deductible for a subsequent covered loss while the prior restoration continues, but applies a new one after the earlier restoration ends. Match that rule to the actual event sequence.

A 168-hour waiting period is seven days. For an illustrative business operating every day and losing an assumed $8,000 daily contribution during that period, the exposure is $56,000. This is a cash-flow sensitivity, not a claim calculation: policy definitions, working days, limits, mitigation and actual financial evidence determine any payment. Compare temporary-operation costs with the separate extra-expense limit as well.

Identify the income being insured and the records supporting it. Sales alone are not the recovery measure. The TWIA form defines business income using net income and continuing normal operating expenses. Ask the adviser to reconcile the coverage basis with payroll, saved expenses, seasonality and the restoration schedule. [Income definition](#source-income-endorsement).

For grid and water interruptions, connect the policy review with the facility’s own operating plan. Insurance can complement backup, alternate sourcing and safe shutdown, but coverage should not be assumed for a contractual curtailment. The [Texas power investigation](/research/texas/texas-power-large-load-business-diligence) explains why interruption restrictions need separate diligence.

sections.title: Read the 2026 filing at its actual scope
paragraphs: TWIA’s August announcement said its own 2026 analysis found commercial rates adequate by 4% and linked improved adequacy to lower catastrophe-funding and reinsurance costs following legislation. This is an insurer-specific actuarial assessment. It is not a measured 4% reduction in commercial premiums, a claim about every Texas insurer, or residential evidence applied to a business. [2026 board announcement](#source-rate-action).

TDI lists the commercial annual filing as P-0826-02, state tracking S739761, submitted August 4, 2026, with File and Use status. Preserve that status instead of calling the filing a project-specific quote or a separately dated approval order. A renewal can change when insured values, selected terms, property characteristics or other charges change even when the filed rate change is zero. [Filing register](#source-rate-register).

For difficult placements, distinguish a Texas-licensed carrier from eligible surplus-lines coverage. TDI explains that surplus-lines companies are not licensed by Texas but can be eligible to transact, while the selling agent needs the appropriate license. It also says these insurers do not participate in a guaranty association. Verify the actual carrier and placement; neither illegality nor protection should be inferred from a market label alone. [Surplus-lines guidance](#source-surplus-lines).

Ask for the insurer’s identity, financial evidence, claims contact and the complete form set. Consider insurer strength, terms and service alongside price. This review contains no commercial-premium dataset or loss-frequency analysis, so it makes no statewide price forecast or ranking of carriers.

sections.title: Preserve the contract that the recovery case depends on
paragraphs: TDI’s certificate guidance states that a certificate cannot alter or extend policy coverage. Rights such as cancellation notice depend on the policy, endorsement or applicable law. A certificate holder should obtain the relevant underlying wording rather than treat the certificate as a substitute for the insurance contract. [Certificate guidance](#source-certificates).

Reconcile the purchase or lease requirements with actual insured interests and endorsements. Assign who insures the building, improvements, equipment and income, and who bears deductibles and uninsured repair. An agreement promising insurance does not itself show that the issued policy grants every promised right.

Maintain the complete declarations, forms, endorsements, schedules, effective dates and binding evidence. Retain asset and financial records off-site or in recoverable systems, with a practical loss-documentation process. Ask the broker and operations team to explain the same event from first damage through payment and restart, identifying any unresolved condition.

Recheck after a renewal or endorsement, changed carrier or insured value, acquisition or major alteration, new TWIA filing or eligibility requirement, revised flood terms, and any changed operating dependency. The decision checklist below is a proposed operating control, not a certification that the business is fully insured.
bullets: Match insured entities, locations and property schedules to the actual operating structure.
Test wind, flood, equipment and utility events using the relevant policy and exclusions.
Normalize settlement values, deductible denominators, sublimits and any reporting conditions.
Model retained physical loss and interruption liquidity separately from premium savings.
Verify daily and total business-income limits, time deductibles and extra-expense terms.
Confirm carrier eligibility, issued endorsements, effective dates and a reproducible claims record.

faqs.question: Does commercial windstorm insurance also cover flood damage?
faqs.answer: Do not assume it does. TWIA provides wind and hail coverage and its commercial form excludes specified flood and surge causes. Assess the separate flood contract and limits. [TWIA scope](#source-wind-eligibility); [commercial form](#source-commercial-form).

faqs.question: Does NFIP commercial flood insurance pay business-interruption losses?
faqs.answer: NFIP guidance excludes business interruption and loss of use. It separately publishes up to $500,000 building and $500,000 contents limits for non-residential coverage. Recovery income needs a separate review. [NFIP coverage](#source-flood-coverage).

faqs.question: Does TWIA’s zero rate-change filing mean my business premium cannot increase?
faqs.answer: No. The filing describes TWIA’s rate action, not the business’s selected insured values, terms or total renewal charge. Obtain the actual quote and reconcile its inputs. [2026 filing](#source-rate-register).

faqs.question: Is a certificate enough to prove the insurance a lease requires?
faqs.answer: A certificate cannot extend the policy. Inspect the applicable forms and issued endorsements for the insured interests and rights the agreement requires. [TDI certificate guidance](#source-certificates).
